chunks.title: Anisocoria: which pupil is bad?
chunks.tldr: Bigger difference in light → big pupil is abnormal (Adie, III palsy, drops, sphincter damage). Bigger in dark → small pupil is abnormal (Horner, miotic, iritis). Same in light and dark, <2 mm, normal reactions → physiological. Always check lids, motility, proptosis.
points: Big pupil, no III signs → pilocarpine 0.125%: Adie constricts (denervation hypersensitivity).
No response → pilocarpine 1%: normal/III palsy constrict; pharmacological block (atropine, scopolamine patch, ipratropium nebuliser) doesn't.
Acute Adie may not yet be hypersensitive.
Slit lamp: torn sphincter, TIDs (trauma).
chunks.hook: Light shows the big bad pupil; dark shows the small bad pupil.

cards.q: Dilated pupil fails to constrict with 1% pilocarpine — diagnosis?
cards.a: Pharmacological mydriasis (anticholinergic exposure).

chunks.title: Horner syndrome
chunks.tldr: Mild ptosis (2 mm) + reverse ptosis + miosis, anisocoria worse in dark (dilation lag), ± anhidrosis, heterochromia if congenital. Confirm: apraclonidine reverses anisocoria (Horner pupil becomes bigger) or cocaine 10% (Horner dilates less). Hydroxyamphetamine: no dilation = 3rd-order. New painful Horner = carotid dissection until proven otherwise → urgent CTA/MRA.
points: 1st order: stroke (Wallenberg), MS, tumour.
2nd order: Pancoast (arm/shoulder pain), thyroid, aortic aneurysm; kids: neuroblastoma.
3rd order: carotid dissection, cluster headache, cavernous sinus, zoster.
Dissection: neck/face pain, pulsatile tinnitus, dysgeusia, TVL → antiplatelets.
Image the whole pathway: MRI brain/neck, chest CT apex, CTA/MRA neck.
Don't do hydroxyamphetamine within 24–48 h of cocaine/apraclonidine.
chunks.hook: Painful new Horner = dissection. Image the neck today.

cards.q: Effect of apraclonidine in Horner syndrome?
cards.a: Horner pupil dilates (denervation α1 supersensitivity) → anisocoria reverses.

cards.q: Horner + ipsilateral arm pain?
cards.a: Pancoast (lung apex) tumour.

chunks.title: Light–near dissociation: Argyll Robertson & Adie
chunks.tldr: Argyll Robertson: small, irregular, bilateral, poor light, good near; vision intact; tertiary syphilis → FTA-ABS/RPR ± LP. Adie: dilated, unilateral, young women, sectoral sphincter palsy, vermiform movements, slow tonic near response; supersensitive to pilocarpine 0.125%; gets smaller over years. Holmes–Adie = + areflexia. Parinaud: mid-dilated, lid retraction, upgaze palsy, convergence–retraction nystagmus → MRI (pinealoma).
points: Other LND: bilateral optic neuropathy/retinopathy, aberrant III, diabetes.
Bilateral Adie → screen syphilis, GCA etc.; Adie under age 1 → familial dysautonomia.
Adie Rx: dilute pilocarpine for glare/accommodation.
chunks.hook: AR = Accommodation Reacts (small pupils, syphilis). Adie = big, slow, young woman.

cards.q: Small irregular pupils that constrict to near but not light?
cards.a: Argyll Robertson pupils — tertiary syphilis.

chunks.title: Third nerve palsy
chunks.tldr: Ptosis, eye down and out, can't adduct/elevate/depress; ± dilated pupil. Pupil-involving → PComm aneurysm until proven otherwise: emergency CTA/MRA (catheter angiogram if equivocal). Pupil-sparing complete palsy in a vasculopath = likely microvascular (recovers within 3 months) — most still image. Pain doesn't help tell them apart.
points: Check IV by intorsion of a conjunctival vessel on downgaze.
Superior division: ptosis + poor elevation; inferior division: no adduction/depression ± pupil.
Age ≥55: ESR/CRP/platelets (GCA).
Mimics: MG (no pupil, fatigue), TED, CPEO, INO, skew, orbital inflammation.
Children: tumour, trauma, congenital, ophthalmoplegic migraine; patch with care (amblyopia).
Ischaemic palsies never regenerate aberrantly.
chunks.hook: Blown pupil + ptosis + down-and-out = aneurysm. Scan now.

cards.q: Most common cause of pupil-involving third nerve palsy?
cards.a: Posterior communicating artery aneurysm.

cards.q: Expected course of microvascular third nerve palsy?
cards.a: Resolution within ~3 months; no aberrant regeneration.

chunks.title: Aberrant III regeneration
chunks.tldr: Misrouted III fibres: lid lifts on downgaze/adduction (pseudo-von Graefe), pupil constricts on downgaze/adduction, eye adducts on attempted up/down gaze. Follows trauma, aneurysm, congenital — never microvascular. Primary aberrant regeneration (no previous palsy) = slow cavernous sinus mass (meningioma, carotid aneurysm) → image.
points: Presumed ischaemic palsy develops aberrancy → image.
chunks.hook: Aberrancy means compression or trauma, not diabetes.

cards.q: Primary aberrant regeneration of CN III suggests?
cards.a: Slowly enlarging cavernous sinus lesion (meningioma or intracavernous aneurysm).

chunks.title: Fourth nerve palsy
chunks.tldr: Vertical/torsional diplopia, worse reading; head tilt to opposite shoulder. Parks 3-step: hyper in primary → worse on contralateral gaze → worse on ipsilateral head tilt (Bielschowsky). Commonest causes: trauma, microvascular, congenital (decompensated). Congenital: old photos with tilt, vertical fusional amplitude >6 Δ.
points: Bilateral IV: alternating hypertropia, V-pattern ET, >10° excyclotorsion on double Maddox rod (often after head trauma).
3-step doesn't fit one muscle → skew deviation → image posterior fossa.
MRI if other neuro signs, age <45 without trauma, or 45–55 without vascular risk.
Rx: prism, occlusion; surgery after ≥6 months stable.
chunks.hook: Right IV palsy: right eye high, worse looking left, worse tilting right.

cards.q: Fusional amplitude that suggests a congenital IV palsy?
cards.a: Vertical fusional amplitude greater than 6 prism dioptres.

cards.q: Excyclotorsion >10° on double Maddox rod suggests?
cards.a: Bilateral fourth nerve palsy.

chunks.title: Sixth nerve palsy
chunks.tldr: Horizontal diplopia worse at distance and toward the weak side; abduction deficit, negative forced ductions. Adults: mostly microvascular; also raised ICP (false localising), cavernous sinus, MS, post-LP, GCA. Kids: post-viral (benign), pontine glioma, hydrocephalus, Gradenigo (otitis + VI ± V, VII). Always check discs for papilloedema and corneal sensation.
points: MRI if: age <45 (then LP if negative), 45–55 without risk factors, pain/other signs, cancer history, bilateral, papilloedema; all children.
Mimics: TED, MG, Duane 1, Möbius, blowout, convergence spasm (miosis!), divergence insufficiency.
Review 6-weekly; MRI if not resolved in 3–6 months.
Surgery after 6 months stable; no patching under 11 years.
chunks.hook: Sixth nerve palsy → look at the discs.

cards.q: Gradenigo syndrome?
cards.a: Petrous apicitis from otitis media: VI palsy + facial pain (V) ± VII/VIII.

chunks.title: Seventh nerve palsy
chunks.tldr: Central (stroke): lower face only, forehead spared. Peripheral: whole half-face, lagophthalmos, ± taste, tears, hyperacusis. Bell palsy is commonest but a diagnosis of exclusion; 86% recover in 2 months; prednisone 60 mg × 7 d + taper helps (antivirals optional). Exclude: Ramsay Hunt (vesicles → acyclovir 800 mg 5×/d), CPA tumour, parotid tumour, Lyme, sarcoid, GBS (bilateral), otitis, fracture, mets.
points: Eye care: tears/ointment → moisture chamber/taping → tarsorrhaphy/gold weight.
Check Bell phenomenon, corneal sensation (V + VII = high risk), Schirmer.
Image if other neuro signs, cancer, or not resolved by 3 months.
Synkinesis/crocodile tears = aberrant regeneration (chronic).
Bilateral: GBS, sarcoid, Lyme.
chunks.hook: Forehead spared = brain. Forehead weak = nerve.

cards.q: Facial palsy with forehead sparing — lesion site?
cards.a: Central (upper motor neuron), e.g., contralateral cortical stroke.

cards.q: Facial palsy that hasn't recovered at 3 months — next step?
cards.a: MRI brain (exclude mass, e.g., CPA or parotid tumour).

chunks.title: Cavernous sinus syndrome
chunks.tldr: Any mix of III, IV, VI + V1/V2 pain/numbness + Horner on one side (orbital apex = + optic neuropathy + proptosis). Causes: CCF (direct high-flow after trauma; dural low-flow in hypertensive women >50; corkscrew vessels, raised IOP, big SOV, bruit), tumours (meningioma, pituitary, NPC, perineural SCC, mets), intracavernous aneurysm, mucormycosis (diabetic/DKA, black nasal eschar), pituitary apoplexy, zoster, cavernous sinus thrombosis (septic, bilateral, very sick), Tolosa–Hunt (exclusion).
points: Mucor: admit, emergency CT, amphotericin B (liposomal less nephrotoxic), biopsy + debridement ± exenteration.
Apoplexy: headache, ↓VA, bitemporal field loss → IV steroids + neurosurgery; Sheehan postpartum.
Septic thrombosis: IV antibiotics (Staph aureus), blood cultures; Lemierre = jugular thrombophlebitis.
Tolosa–Hunt: prednisone 80–100 mg; pain persisting >72 h → re-investigate (lymphoma mimics).
Dural AVF with cortical venous drainage → haemorrhage risk; can present with white quiet eye.
CCF glaucoma: aqueous suppressants (PGA/pilocarpine less useful — raised episcleral venous pressure).
Mimics: MG, CPEO, orbital disease, NPC/clivus, PSP, Miller Fisher.
chunks.hook: Diabetic + multiple palsies + black nose = mucor. Act today.

cards.q: Most common Barrow type of carotid–cavernous fistula?
cards.a: Type D (indirect, feeders from both ICA and ECA).

cards.q: First-line drug for rhino-orbital mucormycosis?
cards.a: IV amphotericin B (plus surgical debridement and correction of DKA).

chunks.title: Myasthenia gravis
chunks.tldr: Painless, variable, fatigable ptosis/diplopia, worse end of day. Pupils never involved. Signs: ptosis worse after 1 min upgaze, orbicularis weakness, Cogan lid twitch, can mimic any motility pattern. Tests: ice test (≥2 mm better), rest/sleep test, AChR Ab (often negative in ocular MG), MuSK, single-fibre EMG (most sensitive), edrophonium (with atropine ready). CT chest for thymoma, TFTs.
points: Bulbar/respiratory symptoms → admit: IVIG/plasmapheresis.
Rx: pyridostigmine 30 mg tds → 60 mg qds; then prednisone (start low — can worsen in first 2 weeks), azathioprine, MMF.
Thymectomy for thymoma; helps generalised MG.
Worsened by β-blockers, macrolides, aminoglycosides.
Ocular only for 2–3 years → generalisation unlikely.
5% have Graves; neonates of MG mums can be floppy.
Lambert–Eaton: strength improves with exercise; paraneoplastic (lung).
chunks.hook: Anything with a normal pupil that gets worse with use = myasthenia.

cards.q: Positive ice test result?
cards.a: Ptosis improves by ≥2 mm after 2 minutes of ice over the closed lid.

cards.q: Imaging every new myasthenic needs?
cards.a: CT chest for thymoma.

chunks.title: CPEO & mimics
chunks.tldr: Slow, symmetric ptosis + ophthalmoplegia, rarely diplopia, no diurnal change, normal pupils, weak orbicularis. Must exclude Kearns–Sayre (onset <20 + salt-and-pepper retinopathy + heart block → ECG/cardiology, pacemaker; ragged red fibres). Others: oculopharyngeal dystrophy (dysphagia), MELAS, abetalipoproteinaemia (acanthocytes), Refsum (phytanic acid), PSP (downgaze first, staring, axial rigidity).
points: Edrophonium can trigger heart block in CPEO.
Rx: lubricants, base-down prisms, cautious ptosis surgery/crutches (exposure).
Myotonic dystrophy: Christmas-tree cataract, can't release handshake.
chunks.hook: Young CPEO + pigment in retina → check the heart (Kearns–Sayre).

cards.q: Triad of Kearns–Sayre syndrome?
cards.a: CPEO, pigmentary retinopathy, cardiac conduction block (onset before 20).

chunks.title: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia
chunks.tldr: MLF lesion: weak/slow adduction on the lesion side + abducting nystagmus of the other eye; convergence often preserved. Named for the side that can't adduct. Young + bilateral → MS; old + unilateral → stroke. WEBINO = bilateral, wall-eyed. One-and-a-half: INO + ipsilateral gaze palsy → only contralateral abduction left. MRI brainstem.
points: Subtle INO: slower adducting saccade.
Skew deviation often accompanies; 3-step doesn't isolate a muscle.
MG can mimic exactly — check for ptosis/fatigue.
chunks.hook: Can't adduct + other eye jumps = MLF (MS if young).

cards.q: In one-and-a-half syndrome, which horizontal movement remains?
cards.a: Abduction of the eye contralateral to the lesion.

chunks.title: Optic neuritis
chunks.tldr: 18–45, unilateral loss over days (nadir ~1 week), pain on eye movement (92%), RAPD, colour loss, central/caecocentral field; disc normal (⅔) or swollen (⅓, no haemorrhages). Uhthoff, Pulfrich. MRI brain + orbits with gad in all; AQP4 + MOG antibodies. ONTT: IV methylpred 1 g × 3 d then oral pred 1 mg/kg × 11 d → faster recovery, same final VA, delays MS for 2 yrs. Never oral pred alone (more recurrence).
points: MS risk at 15 yrs: 72% with ≥1 MRI lesion vs 25% with normal MRI.
≥2 lesions → neurology for disease-modifying therapy.

Atypical = older, severe/no recovery, bilateral, no pain, NMOSD features (hiccups, vomiting, itching), long-segment nerve lesion → spine MRI, plasmapheresis if poor steroid response, rituximab/eculizumab.
DDx: NAION (older, painless, altitudinal), compressive, LHON, toxic, papilloedema.
Follow 4–6 weeks then 3–6 monthly.
chunks.hook: Young + painful eye movements + RAPD = optic neuritis → MRI + IV steroids, never oral alone.

cards.q: Why not treat optic neuritis with oral prednisone alone?
cards.a: ONTT showed increased risk of recurrence.

cards.q: 15-year MS risk after optic neuritis with a normal MRI?
cards.a: About 25% (72% with ≥1 lesion).

chunks.title: Papilloedema
chunks.tldr: Bilateral disc swelling from raised ICP: hyperaemic, blurred margins, obscured vessels, flame haemorrhages, lost SVPs. VA, colour, pupils usually normal; enlarged blind spot. Transient obscurations on standing, headache, nausea, VI palsy. Chronic: grey atrophic disc, optociliary shunts, inferonasal field loss. Emergency MRI + MRV (CT if unavailable) → LP with opening pressure.
points: Causes: tumour, hydrocephalus, IIH, haematoma, SAH (Terson), AVM, abscess, meningitis, encephalitis, venous sinus thrombosis.
Pseudopapilloedema (drusen): vessels visible, SVPs present, B-scan/autofluorescence.
Disc swelling DDx: papillitis, malignant hypertension (check BP!), CRVO, NAION, infiltration (leukaemia → urgent), LHON, diabetic papillopathy, TED, amiodarone.
chunks.hook: Two swollen discs + good vision = papilloedema → MRI/MRV today.

cards.q: Typical visual function in early papilloedema?
cards.a: Normal acuity, colour and pupils; enlarged blind spot and transient obscurations.

chunks.title: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
chunks.tldr: Usually obese young women. Headache, transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, diplopia (VI). Diagnosis: papilloedema + normal MRI/MRV + high opening pressure + normal CSF. Drugs: tetracyclines, vitamin A, OCP, lithium, steroid withdrawal, cyclosporine, amiodarone. Rx: weight loss + acetazolamide (250 mg qds → up to 1 g qds). Vision threatened → optic nerve sheath fenestration or shunt; headache-dominant → shunt/venous stenting.
points: Visual fields are the key monitoring test.
Pregnancy: acetazolamide after 20 weeks; no crash dieting.
Children: 50% have a secondary cause.
Follow 3–4-weekly if active, then 3-monthly.
chunks.hook: Young obese woman + whooshing in ears + swollen discs = IIH.

cards.q: Four criteria for IIH diagnosis?
cards.a: Papilloedema, normal neuroimaging incl. MRV, raised LP opening pressure, normal CSF composition (no other neuro signs except VI).

chunks.title: Giant cell arteritis (AAION)
chunks.tldr: ≥55, sudden severe loss (often CF or worse), chalk-white swollen disc, RAPD; headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, PMR, weight loss, fever. May present as CRAO, VI palsy, or TVL first. ESR (men age/2, women (age+10)/2), CRP, platelets. Steroids immediately: methylpred 250 mg IV q6h × 12 doses → prednisone 80–100 mg (≈1 mg/kg). Temporal artery biopsy within 1 week (positive up to 1 month), 2–3 cm segment.
points: Untreated: other eye within 1–7 days.
Negative adequate biopsy + strong suspicion → biopsy the other side.
Taper slowly over ≥6–12 months guided by symptoms + ESR/CRP; increase if they rise.
PPI + bone protection.
Tocilizumab (IL-6R) speeds remission, spares steroid.
CRP doesn't rise with age — more reliable than ESR.
chunks.hook: Old + jaw pain + white swollen disc = steroids before biopsy.

cards.q: Upper normal ESR for a 70-year-old woman?
Within what time after starting steroids should temporal artery biopsy be done?
cards.a: Ideally within 1 week (can stay positive up to ~1 month).

chunks.title: NAION & PION
chunks.tldr: NAION: 40–60, painless sudden loss on waking, segmental hyperaemic disc swelling + flame haemorrhages, altitudinal field, normal ESR/CRP, crowded 'disc at risk' in the other eye (C/D <0.3). Risks: HTN, DM, lipids, sleep apnoea, nocturnal hypotension; PDE-5 warning. Up to 35% progressive. Rx: observe, risk factors, no bedtime antihypertensives; oedema gone by 8 weeks; ~40% improve a bit. PION: normal disc initially; after long surgery (spine, cardiac) with hypotension/anaemia/prone → transfuse, fix BP; or GCA.
points: Always exclude GCA (ESR/CRP/platelets) in anyone ≥50.
Atrophy without cupping afterwards.
chunks.hook: Small crowded disc + woke up with half a field missing = NAION.

cards.q: Fellow-eye feature typical of NAION?
cards.a: Small crowded 'disc at risk' with absent/small cup.

chunks.title: Toxic, compressive & hereditary optic neuropathies
chunks.tldr: Toxic/nutritional: bilateral painless, caecocentral scotomas, temporal pallor; alcohol/tobacco, B1/B12/folate deficiency, ethambutol, linezolid, isoniazid, amiodarone, methanol (acute). Rx: stop agent, thiamine, folate, B12. Compressive: slow, central field + RAPD; MRI orbits/brain; optociliary shunts only with intrinsic nerve lesions (meningioma). LHON: young men, sequential loss, non-leaking peripapillary telangiectasias, mtDNA 11778/3460/14484; idebenone; no smoking/alcohol; cardiac conduction check. Dominant optic atrophy: age ~4, OPA1, tritan defect.
points: Optic glioma: kids, NF1; usually observe, chemo if progressive (avoid RT).
ONSM: stereotactic fractionated RT.
LHON: mothers pass to all; 50–70% sons affected; men can't transmit.
Radiation optic neuropathy: 1–5 yrs after RT, enhancing nerve on MRI.
chunks.hook: LHON: Lad, Loses one eye then the other, Leaky-looking (but not) vessels, maternaL.

cards.q: Most common LHON mutation?
cards.a: mtDNA 11778 (ND4).

cards.q: Colour defect in dominant optic atrophy?
cards.a: Tritan (blue–yellow).

chunks.title: Congenital nystagmus
chunks.tldr: Infantile nystagmus: from 2–3 months, horizontal, same direction in all gazes, dampens with convergence, null point → face turn. Look for cause: albinism (TIDs), aniridia, LCA (flat ERG), ONH, cataracts, achromatopsia. Latent: appears when one eye covered, fast phase toward viewing eye (fog, don't occlude, for VA). Spasmus nutans (6 mo–3 yr, head nod, shimmering asymmetric) → MRI (glioma mimic). Opsoclonus → search for neuroblastoma.
points: Small face turn: prism base toward face turn; large: surgery (Kestenbaum).
Nystagmus blockage: esotropia damps nystagmus.
chunks.hook: Shimmering eyes + head nodding → MRI. Dancing eyes → find the neuroblastoma.

cards.q: How should acuity be tested in latent nystagmus?
cards.a: Fog the other eye with plus lenses rather than occluding it.

chunks.title: Acquired nystagmus: where's the lesion?
chunks.tldr: Downbeat → cervicomedullary junction (Chiari), cerebellar degeneration — sagittal MRI. Seesaw → parasellar/chiasm (bitemporal field). Convergence–retraction → dorsal midbrain/pineal (Parinaud). Periodic alternating (switches every 60–90 s) → cervicomedullary/posterior fossa; baclofen. Gaze-evoked → alcohol, sedatives, cerebellum. Peripheral vestibular → fast phase away from destructive lesion; with IK = Cogan syndrome. Monocular vertical in a blind eye = Heimann–Bielschowsky.
points: Superior oblique myokymia: monocular torsional oscillopsia; carbamazepine; image rarely.
Oculopalatal myoclonus: old brainstem stroke; oculomasticatory myorhythmia: Whipple.
Bruns (CPA tumour), rebound (cerebellum).
chunks.hook: Down-beat = down at the foramen magnum (Chiari).

cards.q: Seesaw nystagmus localises to?
cards.a: Parasellar/chiasmal region (often with bitemporal hemianopia).

chunks.title: Transient visual loss & vertebrobasilar
chunks.tldr: Amaurosis fugax (monocular, seconds–minutes) = TIA → urgent stroke pathway: MRI DWI, carotid Doppler, echo/ECG, neurology; GCA bloods if ≥50. Look for Hollenhorst plaque. Rx: aspirin, endarterectomy/stent for high-grade stenosis, risk factors. Vertebrobasilar: bilateral blur + vertigo, dysarthria, perioral numbness, drop attacks; check BP both arms (subclavian steal).
points: DDx: papilloedema obscurations (seconds, postural), GCA, impending CRVO, migraine aura (10–50 min, positive phenomena), intermittent angle closure, UGH, drusen, gaze-evoked (orbital mass).
Cover each eye — monocular vs homonymous?
Vasospasm diagnosis of exclusion → calcium channel blocker.
chunks.hook: Curtain over one eye for minutes = mini-stroke → stroke unit today.

cards.q: Workup of amaurosis fugax seen within days?
cards.a: Emergency stroke referral: MRI DWI, carotid duplex, cardiac evaluation (ECG/echo), ± GCA bloods.

chunks.title: Cortical blindness & nonphysiological loss
chunks.tldr: Cortical blindness: severe bilateral loss, normal pupils; bilateral occipital infarcts, PRES, toxins. Anton (denies blindness), Riddoch (sees movement). MRI, stroke workup. Nonphysiological: no findings + normal pupils. Tricks: no RAPD with claimed unilateral loss, mirror test, OKN drum, base-out prism, vertical prism dissociation, Worth 4-dot, start at 20/10 and work up, fog test, half the distance should double acuity, tunnel fields on Goldmann.
points: Don't accuse — offer a 'way out'; reassure vision will recover.
Children: 'magic drops' + reward.
Can't prove it? Re-check 1–2 weeks; ERG, VEP, OCT, MRI.
Mimics: amblyopia, retrobulbar neuritis (RAPD), cone dystrophy, chiasmal tumour, CAR/MAR (abnormal ERG/OCT).
chunks.hook: Claims one blind eye but no RAPD → test for nonorganic loss.

cards.q: Patient with 20/100 at 20 ft reads 20/100 at 10 ft — interpretation?
cards.a: Inconsistent (should be 20/50) → suggests nonphysiological visual loss.

chunks.title: Headache red flags
chunks.tldr: Red flags: age ≥55 with GCA symptoms, disc swelling, fever, altered mentation, stiff neck, ↓vision, neuro signs, subhyaloid haemorrhages. Suspicious: new headache, worst ever, always same side, wakes from sleep, projectile vomiting, aura after headache. Dangerous causes: GCA, acute angle closure, ocular ischaemia, malignant HTN, raised ICP, meningitis/abscess, tumour/aneurysm/AVM, SAH (Terson), haematoma.
points: 'Sinus headache' in diabetic/immunosuppressed → think mucor.
Absent SVPs means little (20% of normals lack them).
Check BP, temperature, temporal arteries, IOP, discs, fields.
chunks.hook: Headache + swollen disc / fever / old age / bad vision = never 'just a headache'.

cards.q: Headache with subhyaloid haemorrhages suggests?
cards.a: Subarachnoid haemorrhage (Terson syndrome).

chunks.title: Migraine & cluster
chunks.tldr: Migraine: 4–72 h, unilateral throbbing, nausea, photo/phonophobia; aura (zig-zags) builds over 5 min, lasts 5–60 min, then headache. Acephalgic = aura only. Image if new after 50, always same side, aura after headache, hemiplegic (sporadic). Abortive: NSAIDs → triptans/gepants; prophylaxis if ≥2/month. Cluster: men, stabbing orbital pain minutes–hours, 1–2×/day for weeks, tearing, rhinorrhoea, Horner, wakes from sleep; alcohol trigger. Rx: 100% O₂ 5–8 L/min, SC sumatriptan; verapamil prophylaxis.
points: Paroxysmal hemicrania: <30 min, many/day, indomethacin-responsive.
SUNCT: seconds, up to 100+/day, prominent autonomic signs.
Ophthalmoplegic 'migraine' in kids = CN III enhancement (inflammatory).
Avoid opioids in migraine.
chunks.hook: Cluster = Clockwork, men, one eye streaming, oxygen fixes it.

cards.q: First-line abortive therapy for cluster headache?
cards.a: High-flow 100% oxygen (or subcutaneous sumatriptan).

cards.q: Headache that responds dramatically to indomethacin?
cards.a: Chronic paroxysmal hemicrania.
